newsitem.title: UK: Sterling breaks 2.86 marks, new gains seen.
newsitem.headline: Sterling breaks 2.86 marks, new gains seen.

text.p: Sterling raced to fresh 58-month peaks above 2.86 marks on Friday and analysts say the British unit shows no signs of running out of steam.
"Near-term there is still upwards pressure on sterling and I can see that intensifying," said Adam Cole, economist at HSBC James Capel.
"We could see it peak at 2.90 and I wouldn't even rule out 3.00 deutschmarks."
Upward pressure on British interest rates, widespread expectations of a broad-based euro in 1999 and a softer outlook for the U.S dollar will keep sterling poised for higher ground, analysts said.
Sterling/mark forged to fresh 58-month peaks of 2.8605 marks on Friday. At 1330 GMT it stood at 2.8595/05 marks.

The pound's index against a trade-weighted basket of currencies shot on Friday to its highest level since September 1992. Since August, sterling has risen some 19 percent against against the basket of currencies - hampering British exporters in its wake.
"If you're an exporter, there doesn't look like being too much sunshine on the horizon for at least the next six months," said Jeremy Stretch, currency strategist at NatWest Markets.
Markets, however, are expecting the pound to get some respite if Chancellor Gordon Brown's debut budget, the first Labour budget in Britain for 18 years, is tough on fiscal policy.

With economic data pointing to rampant economic growth, markets are expecting Brown to be tough on fiscal policy. If Brown is lenient on taxes, the newly-independent Bank of England monetary committee will probably compensate by upping base rates even further, said analysts.

"I think Brown would like to see quite significant tax increases, but having fought the election on taxes Blair is keen to play the honest broker and is likely to stamp on the sort of increases you'd need to take pressure off interest rates," said Cole.
Cole said only a moderate fiscal tightening could mean interest rates going as high as eight percent by the second half of 1998. On June 6 the BoE hiked rates to 6.50 percent.

A strong rise in May retail sales - a key indicator of consumer demand - and a report showing PSBR was marginally higher than previously thought have increased the pressure for a tough budget, said analysts.

NatWest's Stretch said fiscal tightening of three billion stg would be the minimum needed to quell expectations of hefty rate rises. A policy mix below that would not be sufficient to take the upward pressure off rates, he said.

That will keep sterling well supported against European currencies as contenders for monetary union aim for stable interest rates to speed up debt repayments and get their budgets within Maastrict limits.
Analysts also predict steady rates in the United States where economic data has relieved concern of an overheating economy.
But economists say the pound could be heading for a fall in the long term if the budget fails to put the brakes on Britain's buoyant economy and inflation begins to weigh on the currency.
"Longer-term I'm much more bearish for sterling," said Cole.
"Over the long-term I'm worried the UK will have a poor inflationary performance compared to the rest of Europe and the market might start to worry about the consequences of that."
